title: "Building eolas: a data platform for New Zealand official statistics"
subtitle: "What it takes to make public data actually usable"
author: "Phil Donovan"
date: "2026-07-21"
categories: [data-engineering, iceberg, singer, aws, new-zealand]

New Zealand publishes a lot of good official data. Getting hold of it is the tedious part.

Stats NZ has one portal, the Reserve Bank has another, LINZ has a third. MBIE, MSD, Police
and NZTA each do their own thing. Councils publish through ArcGIS services with wildly
varying conventions. Some sources offer a clean API. Others offer a CSV behind a form, or
an Excel file with merged header cells and a footnote in row 4. The OECD has a proper SDMX
API, which is a relief until you read the specification.

None of this is unusual, and none of it is anyone's fault. Agencies publish for their own
purposes and their own audiences. But the practical result is that a good chunk of any
analysis project gets spent on retrieval and cleaning before the actual work starts. I have
done that work often enough, in consulting and in government, that I got tired of doing it
again.

eolas is my attempt to do it once. It is a platform that pulls together over 700 datasets
from New Zealand, Australian and OECD sources, cleans them to a consistent shape, and serves
them through a single typed API with Python and R clients and a CLI. This post covers how it
is built and which decisions turned out to matter.

## Three planes

It helps to think of the system in three parts: getting data in, storing it, and serving it
out.

**Getting data in.** Each source has its own tap, written to the Singer specification. Singer
defines a simple contract between a tap (which extracts) and a target (which loads), and the
useful property is that it makes every source a small, independently testable unit. A tap for
RBNZ interest rates has nothing to do with a tap for LINZ parcels, and neither can break the
other. Councils are the exception to the one-tap-per-source rule: enough of them publish
through ArcGIS that a single generic base tap covers most, parameterised per council.

Meltano orchestrates the taps. They run as scheduled ECS Fargate tasks, triggered by
EventBridge, with one task definition per pipeline grouped by refresh cadence. Daily sources
run daily; quarterly ones do not.

**Storing it.** Everything lands in Apache Iceberg tables on S3, catalogued in AWS Glue. A
custom loader, `target-iceberg`, handles the write.

**Serving it out.** Two FastAPI applications share one codebase. One serves the marketing site,
dashboard, authentication and billing. The other serves the data API. They run on ECS Fargate
behind an ALB, with Cloudflare in front, and a Postgres database on RDS holds customer and
account data.

## The decisions that mattered

Most architectural choices are reversible and not worth much discussion. A few were not.

### An open table format

Choosing Iceberg on object storage rather than loading everything into a warehouse was the
call that shaped everything downstream. It means the same physical data can be read three
ways without copying it: through the eolas API, through a Snowflake zero-copy share, and
directly by anything that speaks Iceberg, such as dbt, Athena or pyiceberg.

The Snowflake share is the clearest illustration. Customers on Snowflake query our S3 and
Glue directly. There is no nightly sync job, no second copy drifting out of date, and no
Snowflake warehouse of our own to pay for. Column documentation and table descriptions are
materialised into the Glue catalog, so someone browsing the share sees the same clean names
and definitions as someone reading the API docs.

The cost is that Iceberg is a lower level of abstraction than a managed warehouse. You think
about compaction, snapshot expiry and manifest files. For a platform whose product is the
data itself, that seemed like the right trade.

### Keeping history

Official statistics get restated. A quarterly figure published in March may be revised in
June, and a dataset that looks static will quietly change underneath you. If you overwrite on
each load, you lose the ability to answer what a series looked like at a point in time, which
is exactly the question an analyst reproducing a published result needs to ask.

So `target-iceberg` keeps slowly changing dimension history rather than overwriting. Deletes
expire a row, additions append a new one, and the full history stays queryable.

This has been the single largest source of subtle bugs in the project. The failure mode is
nasty because it is quiet: a bookmark handled wrongly, or a merge that takes the wrong branch,
does not raise an error. It just writes less data than it should, and you find out weeks later
when someone asks why a series has a hole in it. The fix was not cleverness in the merge logic
but canaries around it. Loads now check for unexpected shrinkage and compare against source
fidelity, and fail loudly when the numbers do not line up.

If I were starting again, I would write those checks first.

### Keeping batch away from serving

Early on, extraction ran on the same box that served the API. This works until a large backfill
runs, at which point the box becomes unresponsive and the API goes with it. Moving batch onto
Fargate fixed it permanently, and had the side benefit of making pipeline scheduling a
first-class thing rather than a crontab.

A related lesson, less architectural and more practical: the ETL image builds in CI and pushes
to ECR. Building and pushing locally wedged the Docker daemon often enough that I made it a
rule.

### Outgrowing SQLite

Customer and account data started in SQLite on the application box. This was fine for a single
instance and became the binding constraint on everything else. One writer, one host, backups
that amount to copying a file, and foreign keys that are more suggestion than guarantee. It
also made horizontal scaling impossible, because two application instances cannot share a
local file.

Moving to Postgres on RDS was the enabler for running more than one instance, which in turn was
the enabler for high availability. The migration itself was unremarkable, done with SQLAlchemy
Core and Alembic, with a reversible cutover gated on smoke tests. The lesson is not about the
mechanics. It is that a storage choice made for convenience early on quietly set a ceiling that
had to be removed before anything else could improve.

## Where it is now

The platform runs across multiple availability zones, with rolling deploys gated on a readiness
check, and a transform layer built on dbt against Athena producing derived marts as Iceberg
tables. The first of those joins parcels and titles with council hazard and zoning data, which
is the sort of question that is straightforward to ask and genuinely tedious to assemble from
source.

There is a reasonable amount still to do. More sources, better coverage of the ones already
there, and continued work on the contract tests that keep the whole thing honest.

If you work with New Zealand data and want to look, the platform is at
[eolas.fyi](https://eolas.fyi), and the Python and R clients are on
[GitHub](https://github.com/phildonovan).
